name: Notification System
tagline: Events in, rate-limited fan-out to push, email and SMS workers, failures dead-lettered
summary: Any service publishes a notification event to Kafka. A dispatcher applies user preferences, deduplicates and rate-limits with Redis, then places a job on a per-channel RabbitMQ queue. Push, email and SMS workers call providers with retries; messages that keep failing land in a dead-letter queue instead of blocking the channel.

nodes.label: Producing Services
nodes.why: Orders, chat, billing — any service publishes 'notify user X about Y' and never learns how delivery works.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Absorbs bursts (a marketing blast, a flash sale) durably and lets the dispatcher fall behind without producers noticing.

nodes.label: Dispatcher
nodes.why: Decides whether, how and when a user is notified: honours opt-outs, drops duplicates, throttles noisy senders and picks channels.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Sliding-window counters per user and per template, plus short-TTL keys of recently sent event ids, need atomic sub-millisecond operations.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ
nodes.why: One queue per channel with acknowledgements, retry delays and dead-letter exchanges — exactly the work-queue semantics channel workers need.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Opt-outs, quiet hours, device tokens and a record of what was sent must be durable and queryable.

nodes.label: Push Worker
nodes.why: Handles device-token errors and provider rate limits independently of email and SMS.

nodes.label: Email Worker
nodes.why: Renders templates and submits to the provider; bounces and throttling are handled here.

nodes.label: SMS Worker
nodes.why: The most expensive channel, so it is rate-limited most strictly and scaled separately.

nodes.label: Delivery Providers
nodes.role: APNs, FCM, email and SMS APIs
nodes.why: Third-party services with their own quotas, outages and error codes; every call is a candidate for retry, backoff and circuit breaking.

nodes.label: Dead Letter Queue
nodes.why: An invalid device token or a permanently bouncing address must not be retried forever; parking it keeps the channel queue flowing and gives operators something to inspect.

flows.name: Send a notification
steps: The order service publishes NotificationRequested { userId, template, payload, eventId }.
Kafka stores it in the notifications topic; the producer is done.
The dispatcher consumes it and starts the routing decision.
Preferences and device tokens are loaded from PostgreSQL — the user allows push but has opted out of SMS.
Redis checks the eventId was not seen before and increments the user's hourly counter; both pass.
A push job is placed on the push queue in RabbitMQ.
The push worker takes the job and builds the provider request.
APNs or FCM accepts the message and the worker acknowledges the job.

flows.name: Provider failure and dead-lettering
steps: An email job is delivered to the email worker.
The worker submits it and receives a 5xx; it rejects the job so RabbitMQ redelivers after a backoff delay.
The provider keeps failing for this address across three attempts.
RabbitMQ moves the job to the dead-letter queue; operators inspect it later while other emails keep flowing.

flows.name: Rate limit a noisy sender
steps: A bug makes a service publish the same alert 500 times in a minute.
The dispatcher processes each event as usual.
Redis reports the eventId as already seen, or the per-user window as exhausted; the dispatcher drops or delays the extras and records the decision.

decisions.decision: Kafka for ingest, RabbitMQ for channel work queues
decisions.why: Ingest needs to absorb huge bursts durably and let several consumers (dispatcher, analytics) read the same stream. Channel delivery needs per-message acknowledgement, delayed retries and dead-letter routing, which RabbitMQ provides natively.
decisions.tradeoff: Two brokers to operate and reason about. A smaller system would pick one — RabbitMQ end to end is perfectly adequate below tens of thousands of notifications per minute.

decisions.decision: Rate limiting and deduplication in Redis
decisions.why: Every notification requires an atomic counter increment and a set-if-not-exists check; these must be fast and shared across dispatcher instances.
decisions.tradeoff: Counters are lost if Redis is not persisted, so a restart briefly allows over-sending. Doing this in PostgreSQL is durable but adds write load to every event.

decisions.decision: Dead-letter after a bounded number of retries
decisions.why: Some failures are permanent (bad token, unsubscribed address). Retrying them forever burns provider quota and blocks healthy messages behind them.
decisions.tradeoff: Dead-lettered messages need an owner and a process — a DLQ nobody watches is just a slower way of losing messages.

versions.title: Direct calls
versions.summary: Each service calls the email and push providers itself. Simple until a provider outage slows every service down.

versions.title: Queue and workers
versions.summary: Producers publish events; a dispatcher routes them to per-channel queues and workers call providers.

versions.title: Preferences, limits and DLQ
versions.summary: Preferences and templates move to PostgreSQL, Redis rate-limits and deduplicates, and a dead-letter queue catches messages that keep failing.

textAlternative: Producing services at the top publish notification events to Kafka. A dispatcher below it consumes them, reads preferences from PostgreSQL on the right, checks deduplication and rate-limit counters in Redis on the left, and places channel jobs on RabbitMQ. Three workers beneath RabbitMQ — push, email and SMS — take jobs and call external delivery providers at the bottom. Jobs that exhaust their retries are moved to a dead-letter queue on the right.
